2. Emit ===NOTHING=== ONLY when the log itself contains no durable knowledge
   (e.g. "FLUSH_OK", or purely transient chatter). "An article already covers
   this topic" is NOT a reason to emit ===NOTHING=== - it is a reason to UPDATE
   that article with whatever this log adds.
3. Every article: complete YAML frontmatter (title, sources, created, updated)
   with `sources` citing 2026-09-26.md; at least 2 [[wikilinks]]; Key Points
   3-5 bullets; Details 2+ paragraphs; Related Concepts 2+ entries; encyclopedia
   style — neutral and comprehensive. Follow the AGENTS.md article format exactly.
4. Create a connection article when the log reveals a non-obvious relationship
   between 2+ concepts.
4b. Do NOT re-emit an article whose only change would be the `updated:` date or
   a restatement of what it already says. Measured on a real run, 4 of 5
   "updates" changed nothing but the timestamp - that is churn: it rewrites
   files, dirties backups, and invalidates caches while adding no knowledge.
   Re-emit an article only when you are adding substantive content.
5. Add one ===INDEX=== table row per article (new or updated).

Emit ONLY the delimiter blocks — no preamble, no commentary.

message.content:
You are a knowledge compiler. Your job is to read a daily conversation log
and extract knowledge into structured wiki articles.

## Schema (AGENTS.md)

# AGENTS.md - Personal Knowledge Base Schema

> Adapted from [Andrej Karpathy's LLM Knowledge Base](https://gist.github.com/karpathy/442a6bf555914893e9891c11519de94f) architecture.
> Instead of ingesting external articles, this system compiles knowledge from your own AI conversations.

## The Compiler Analogy

```
daily/          = source code    (your conversations - the raw material)
LLM             = compiler       (extracts and organizes knowledge)
knowledge/      = executable     (structured, queryable knowledge base)
lint            = test suite     (health checks for consistency)
memlint         = test suite     (same, for the memory files loaded each session)
queries         = runtime        (using the knowledge)
```

You don't manually organize your knowledge. You have conversations, and the LLM handles the synthesis, cross-referencing, and maintenance.

---

## Architecture

### Layer 1: `daily/` - Conversation Logs (Immutable Source)

Daily logs capture what happened in your AI coding sessions. These are the "raw sources" - append-only, never edited after the fact.

```
daily/
├── 2026-04-01.md
├── 2026-04-02.md
├── ...
```

Each file follows this format:

```markdown
# Daily Log: YYYY-MM-DD

## Sessions

### Session (HH:MM) - Brief Title

**Context:** What the user was working on.

**Key Exchanges:**
- User asked about X, assistant explained Y
- Decided to use Z approach because...
- Discovered that W doesn't work when...

**Decisions Made:**
- Chose library X over Y because...
- Architecture: went with pattern Z

**Lessons Learned:**
- Always do X before Y to avoid...
- The gotcha with Z is that...

**Action Items:**
- [ ] Follow up on X
- [ ] Refactor Y when time permits
```

### Layer 2: `knowledge/` - Compiled Knowledge (LLM-Owned)

The LLM owns this directory entirely. Humans read it but rarely edit it directly.

```
knowledge/
├── index.md              # Master catalog - every article with one-line summary
├── log.md                # Append-only chronological build log
├── concepts/             # Atomic knowledge articles
├── connections/          # Cross-cutting insights linking 2+ concepts
└── qa/                   # Filed query answers (compounding knowledge)
```

### Layer 3: This File (AGENTS.md)

The schema that tells the LLM how to compile and maintain the knowledge base. This is the "compiler specification."

---

## Structural Files

### `knowledge/index.md` - Master Catalog

A table listing every knowledge article. This is the primary retrieval mechanism - the LLM reads this FIRST when answering any query, then selects relevant articles to read in full.

Format:

```markdown
# Knowledge Base Index

| Article | Summary | Compiled From | Updated |
|---------|---------|---------------|---------|
| [[concepts/supabase-auth]] | Row-level security patterns and JWT gotchas | daily/2026-04-02.md | 2026-04-02 |
| [[connections/auth-and-webhooks]] | Token verification patterns shared across Supabase auth and Stripe webhooks | daily/2026-04-02.md, daily/2026-04-04.md | 2026-04-04 |
```

### `knowledge/log.md` - Build Log

Append-only chronological record of every compile, query, and lint operation.

Format:

```markdown
# Build Log

## [2026-04-01T14:30:00] compile | Daily Log 2026-04-01
- Source: daily/2026-04-01.md
- Articles created: [[concepts/nextjs-project-structure]], [[concepts/tailwind-setup]]
- Articles updated: (none)

## [2026-04-02T09:00:00] query | "How do I handle auth redirects?"
- Consulted: [[concepts/supabase-auth]], [[concepts/nextjs-middleware]]
- Filed to: [[qa/auth-redirect-handling]]
```

---

## Article Formats

### Concept Articles (`knowledge/concepts/`)

One article per atomic piece of knowledge. These are facts, patterns, decisions, preferences, and lessons extracted from your conversations.

```markdown
---
title: "Concept Name"
aliases: [alternate-name, abbreviation]
tags: [domain, topic]
sources:
  - "daily/2026-04-01.md"
  - "daily/2026-04-03.md"
created: 2026-04-01
updated: 2026-04-03
---

# Concept Name

[2-4 sentence core explanation]

## Key Points

- [Bullet points, each self-contained]

## Details

[Deeper explanation, encyclopedia-style paragraphs]

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/related-concept]] - How it connects

## Sources

- [[daily/2026-04-01.md]] - Initial discovery during project setup
- [[daily/2026-04-03.md]] - Updated after debugging session
```

### Connection Articles (`knowledge/connections/`)

Cross-cutting synthesis linking 2+ concepts. Created when a conversation reveals a non-obvious relationship.

```markdown
---
title: "Connection: X and Y"
connects:
  - "concepts/concept-x"
  - "concepts/concept-y"
sources:
  - "daily/2026-04-04.md"
created: 2026-04-04
updated: 2026-04-04
---

# Connection: X and Y

## The Connection

[What links these concepts]

## Key Insight

[The non-obvious relationship discovered]

## Evidence

[Specific examples from conversations]

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/concept-x]]
- [[concepts/concept-y]]
```

### Q&A Articles (`knowledge/qa/`)

Filed answers from queries. Every complex question answered by the system can be permanently stored, making future queries smarter.

```markdown
---
title: "Q: Original Question"
question: "The exact question asked"
consulted:
  - "concepts/article-1"
  - "concepts/article-2"
filed: 2026-04-05
---

# Q: Original Question

## Answer

[The synthesized answer with [[wikilinks]] to sources]

## Sources Consulted

- [[concepts/article-1]] - Relevant because...
- [[concepts/article-2]] - Provided context on...

## Follow-Up Questions

- What about edge case X?
- How does this change if Y?
```

---

## Core Operations

### 1. Compile (daily/ -> knowledge/)

When processing a daily log:

1. Read the daily log file
2. Read `knowledge/index.md` to understand current knowledge state
3. Read existing articles that may need updating
4. For each piece of knowledge found in the log:
   - If an existing concept article covers this topic: UPDATE it with new information, add the daily log as a source
   - If it's a new topic: CREATE a new `concepts/` article
5. If the log reveals a non-obvious connection between 2+ existing concepts: CREATE a `connections/` article
6. UPDATE `knowledge/index.md` with new/modified entries
7. APPEND to `knowledge/log.md`

**Important guidelines:**
- A single daily log may touch 3-10 knowledge articles
- Prefer updating existing articles over creating near-duplicates
- Use Obsidian-style `[[wikilinks]]` with full relative paths from knowledge/
- Write in encyclopedia style - factual, concise, self-contained
- Every article must have YAML frontmatter
- Every article must link back to its source daily logs

### 2. Query (Ask the Knowledge Base)

1. Read `knowledge/index.md` (the master catalog)
2. Based on the question, identify 3-10 relevant articles from the index
3. Read those articles in full
4. Synthesize an answer with `[[wikilink]]` citations
5. If `--file-back` is specified: create a `knowledge/qa/` article and update index.md and log.md

**Why this works without RAG:** At personal knowledge base scale (50-500 articles), the LLM reading a structured index outperforms cosine similarity. The LLM understands what the question is really asking and selects pages accordingly. Embeddings find similar words; the LLM finds relevant concepts.

### 3. Lint (Health Checks)

Seven checks, run periodically:

1. **Broken links** - `[[wikilinks]]` pointing to non-existent articles
2. **Orphan pages** - Articles with zero inbound links from other articles
3. **Orphan sources** - Daily logs that haven't been compiled yet
4. **Stale articles** - Source daily log changed since article was last compiled
5. **Contradictions** - Conflicting claims across articles (requires LLM judgment)
6. **Missing backlinks** - A links to B but B doesn't link back to A
7. **Sparse articles** - Below 200 words, likely incomplete

Output: a markdown report with severity levels (error, warning, suggestion).

---

## Conventions

- **Wikilinks:** Use Obsidian-style `[[path/to/article]]` without `.md` extension
- **Writing style:** Encyclopedia-style, factual, third-person where appropriate
- **Dates:** ISO 8601 (YYYY-MM-DD for dates, full ISO for timestamps in log.md)
- **File naming:** lowercase, hyphens for spaces (e.g., `supabase-row-level-security.md`)
- **Frontmatter:** Every article must have YAML frontmatter with at minimum: title, sources, created, updated
- **Sources:** Always link back to the daily log(s) that contributed to an article

---

## Full Project Structure

```
llm-personal-kb/
|-- .claude/
|   |-- settings.json                # Hook configuration (auto-activates in Claude Code)
|-- .gitignore                       # Excludes runtime state, temp files, caches
|-- AGENTS.md                        # This file - schema + full technical reference
|-- README.md                        # Concise overview + quick start
|-- pyproject.toml                   # Dependencies (at root so hooks can find it)
|-- daily/                           # "Source code" - conversation logs (immutable)
|-- knowledge/                       # "Executable" - compiled knowledge (LLM-owned)
|   |-- index.md                     #   Master catalog - THE retrieval mechanism
|   |-- log.md                       #   Append-only build log
|   |-- concepts/                    #   Atomic knowledge articles
|   |-- connections/                 #   Cross-cutting insights linking 2+ concepts
|   |-- qa/                          #   Filed query answers (compounding knowledge)
|-- scripts/                         # CLI tools
|   |-- compile.py                   #   Compile daily logs -> knowledge articles
|   |-- query.py                     #   Ask questions (index-guided, no RAG)
|   |-- lint.py                      #   7 health checks (knowledge base)
|   |-- memlint.py                   #   6 health checks (memory tier)
|   |-- flush.py                     #   Extract memories from conversations (background)
|   |-- config.py                    #   Path constants
|   |-- utils.py                     #   Shared helpers
|-- hooks/                           # Claude Code hooks
|   |-- session-start.py             #   Injects knowledge into every session
|   |-- session-end.py               #   Extracts conversation -> daily log
|   |-- pre-compact.py               #   Safety net: captures context before compaction
|-- reports/                         # Lint reports (gitignored)
```

---

## Hook System (Automatic Capture)

Hooks are configured in `.claude/settings.json` and fire automatically when you use Claude Code in this project.

### `.claude/settings.json` Format

```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "SessionStart": [{ "matcher": "", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "uv run python hooks/session-start.py", "timeout": 15 }] }],
    "PreCompact": [{ "matcher": "", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "uv run python hooks/pre-compact.py", "timeout": 10 }] }],
    "SessionEnd": [{ "matcher": "", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "uv run python hooks/session-end.py", "timeout": 10 }] }]
  }
}
```

Commands use simple relative paths from the project root. Empty `matcher` catches all events.

### Hook Details

**`session-start.py`** (SessionStart)
- Pure local I/O, no API calls, runs in under 1 second
- Reads `knowledge/index.md` and the most recent daily log
- Outputs JSON to stdout: `{"hookSpecificOutput": {"hookEventName": "SessionStart", "additionalContext": "..."}}`
- Claude sees the knowledge base index at the start of every session
- Max context: 20,000 characters

**`session-end.py`** (SessionEnd)
- Reads hook input from stdin (JSON with `session_id`, `transcript_path`, `cwd`)
- Copies the raw JSONL transcript to a temp file (no parsing in the hook - keeps it fast)
- Spawns `flush.py` as a fully detached background process
- Recursion guard: exits immediately if `CLAUDE_INVOKED_BY` env var is set

**`pre-compact.py`** (PreCompact)
- Same architecture as session-end.py
- Fires before Claude Code auto-compacts the context window
- Guards against empty `transcript_path` (known Claude Code bug #13668)
- Critical for long sessions: captures context before summarization discards it

**Why both PreCompact and SessionEnd?** Long-running sessions may trigger multiple auto-compactions before you close the session. Without PreCompact, intermediate context is lost to summarization before SessionEnd ever fires.

### Background Flush Process (`flush.py`)

Spawned by both hooks as a fully detached background process:
- **Windows:** `CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP | DETACHED_PROCESS` flags
- **Mac/Linux:** `start_new_session=True`

This ensures flush.py survives after Claude Code's hook process exits.

**What flush.py does:**
1. Sets `CLAUDE_INVOKED_BY=memory_flush` env var (prevents recursive hook firing)
2. Reads the pre-extracted conversation context from the temp `.md` file
3. Skips if context is empty or if same session was flushed within 60 seconds (deduplication)
4. Calls Claude Agent SDK (`query()` with `allowed_tools=[]`, `max_turns=2`)
5. Claude decides what's worth saving - returns structured bullet points or `FLUSH_OK`
6. Appends result to `daily/YYYY-MM-DD.md`
7. Cleans up temp context file
8. **End-of-day auto-compilation:** If it's past 6 PM local time (`COMPILE_AFTER_HOUR = 18`) and today's daily log has changed since its last compilation (hash comparison against `state.json`), spawns `compile.py` as another detached background process. This means compilation happens automatically once a day without needing a cron job or manual trigger.

### JSONL Transcript Format

Claude Code stores conversations as `.jsonl` files. Messages are nested under a `message` key:

```python
entry = json.loads(line)
msg = entry.get("message", {})
role = msg.get("role", "")     # "user" or "assistant"
content = msg.get("content", "")  # string or list of content blocks
```

Content can be a string or a list of blocks (`{"type": "text", "text": "..."}` dicts).

---

## Script Details

### compile.py - The Compiler

Uses the Claude Agent SDK's async streaming `query()`:

```python
async for message in query(
    prompt=compile_prompt,
    options=ClaudeAgentOptions(
        cwd=str(ROOT_DIR),
        system_prompt={"type": "preset", "preset": "claude_code"},
        allowed_tools=["Read", "Write", "Edit", "Glob", "Grep"],
        permission_mode="acceptEdits",
        max_turns=30,
    ),
):
```

- Builds a prompt with: AGENTS.md schema, current index, all existing articles, and the daily log
- Claude reads the daily log, decides what concepts to extract, and writes files directly
- `permission_mode="acceptEdits"` auto-approves all file operations
- Incremental: tracks SHA-256 hashes of daily logs in `state.json`, skips unchanged files
- Cost: ~$0.45-0.65 per daily log (increases as KB grows)

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/compile.py              # compile new/changed only
uv run python scripts/compile.py --all        # force recompile everything
uv run python scripts/compile.py --file daily/2026-04-01.md
uv run python scripts/compile.py --dry-run
```

### query.py - Index-Guided Retrieval

Loads the entire knowledge base into context (index + all articles). No RAG.

At personal KB scale (50-500 articles), the LLM reading a structured index outperforms vector similarity. The LLM understands what you're really asking; cosine similarity just finds similar words.

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/query.py "What auth patterns do I use?"
uv run python scripts/query.py "What's my error handling strategy?" --file-back
```

With `--file-back`, creates a Q&A article in `knowledge/qa/` and updates the index and log. This is the compounding loop - every question makes the KB smarter.

### lint.py - Health Checks

Seven checks:

| Check | Type | Catches |
|-------|------|---------|
| Broken links | Structural | `[[wikilinks]]` to non-existent articles |
| Orphan pages | Structural | Articles with zero inbound links |
| Orphan sources | Structural | Daily logs not yet compiled |
| Stale articles | Structural | Source logs changed since compilation |
| Missing backlinks | Structural | A links to B but B doesn't link back |
| Sparse articles | Structural | Under 200 words |
| Contradictions | LLM | Conflicting claims across articles |

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/lint.py                    # all checks
uv run python scripts/lint.py --structural-only  # skip LLM check (free)
```

Reports saved to `reports/lint-YYYY-MM-DD.md`.

### memlint.py - Memory Tier Health Checks

`lint.py` stops at `knowledge/`. The files the harness actually injects into every
session live elsewhere and were never audited: `~/.claude/global-memory/` and the
active `~/.claude/projects/*/memory/` slugs. Drift there is the most expensive
drift in the system, because it is read at the start of every conversation.

Seven checks:

| Check | Type | Catches |
|-------|------|---------|
| Index drift | Structural | Memory file missing from MEMORY.md, or an index pointer with no file |
| Broken links | Structural | `[[links]]` that do not match any frontmatter `name:` in the slug |
| Name form | Structural | `name:` that is not the bare kebab stem (type belongs in `metadata.type`) |
| Near-duplicates | Structural | Within-slug TF-IDF similarity above the threshold |
| Cap overruns | Structural | A file past the character cap it declares in its own header |
| Content in index | Structural | Facts written into MEMORY.md, which is meant to hold pointers |
| Contradictions | LLM | Conflicting, redundant, or superseded claims across memory files |

**Scope.** Retired `C--Users-eric-rash*` slugs are excluded everywhere - the macOS
slugs were re-keyed from them, so including them reports history as duplication.
`handoffs/` and `transcripts/` are session records, not memory, and are never linted.
The LLM check defaults to `global-memory` + the `DEV` and `~` slugs, the ones that
load together in a working session; `--all-slugs` widens it.

**Similarity threshold.** Default 0.45. Measured 2026-09-01: the highest genuine
within-slug pair scored 0.33. The report always prints the top pairs per slug so
the number can be retuned against evidence.

**Report only.** memlint never edits a memory file. Merging and deleting memories
stays a human decision.

**CLI:**
```bash
uv run python scripts/memlint.py                    # all checks
uv run python scripts/memlint.py --structural-only  # skip LLM check (free)
uv run python scripts/memlint.py --all-slugs        # widen the LLM check
uv run python scripts/memlint.py --threshold 0.6    # retune near-duplicates
```

Reports saved to `reports/memlint-YYYY-MM-DD.md`; `--structural-only` writes
`memlint-YYYY-MM-DD-structural.md` instead, so a free run never clobbers the
day's paid-for LLM findings. Runs automatically after the Sunday 02:30
adjudication job.

---

## State Tracking

`scripts/state.json` tracks:
- `ingested` - map of daily log filenames to SHA-256 hashes, compilation timestamps, and costs
- `query_count` - total queries run
- `last_lint` - timestamp of most recent lint
- `last_memlint` - timestamp of most recent memory-tier lint
- `total_cost` - cumulative API cost

`scripts/last-flush.json` tracks flush deduplication (session_id + timestamp).

Both are gitignored and regenerated automatically.

---

## Dependencies

`pyproject.toml` (at project root):
- `claude-agent-sdk>=0.1.29` - Claude Agent SDK for LLM calls with tool use
- `python-dotenv>=1.0.0` - Environment variable management
- `tzdata>=2024.1` - Timezone data
- Python 3.12+, managed by [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/)

No API key needed - uses Claude Code's built-in credentials at `~/.claude/.credentials.json`.

---

## Costs

| Operation | Cost |
|-----------|------|
| Compile one daily log | $0.45-0.65 |
| Query (no file-back) | ~$0.15-0.25 |
| Query (with file-back) | ~$0.25-0.40 |
| Full lint (with contradictions) | ~$0.15-0.25 |
| Structural lint only | $0.00 |
| Full memlint (with contradictions) | ~$0.15-0.25 |
| Structural memlint only | $0.00 |
| Memory flush (per session) | ~$0.02-0.05 |

---

## Customization

### Additional Article Types

Add directories like `people/`, `projects/`, `tools/` to `knowledge/`. Define the article format in this file (AGENTS.md) and update `utils.py`'s `list_wiki_articles()` to include them.

### Obsidian Integration

The knowledge base is pure markdown with `[[wikilinks]]` - works natively in Obsidian. Point a vault at `knowledge/` for graph view, backlinks, and search.

### Scaling Beyond Index-Guided Retrieval

At ~2,000+ articles / ~2M+ tokens, the index becomes too large for the context window. At that point, add hybrid RAG (keyword + semantic search) as a retrieval layer before the LLM. See Karpathy's recommendation of `qmd` by Tobi Lutke for search at scale.

# Jev/TypeSafe Leverage Sweep Across DEV Projects

On 2026-09-22 a survey was run to identify where TypeSafe's Jev (a System One model) could still add value across Eric's DEV projects, following an earlier leverage sweep that had already measured and dropped eight candidate ideas. The sweep applied three explicit admission conditions to every remaining candidate, producing three survivors and one recommendation. Nothing was built; the session ended holding for a user pick, with "stop hunting and keep only the router plus verifier" recorded as a defensible outcome.

## Key Points

- **Three admission conditions for a Jev build:** (1) the task must be a genuine judgment call, not a lookup, join, or threshold; (2) something downstream must already consume the answer; (3) plain code must have been tried first and measurably fallen short. All three must hold.
- **Three survivors, one recommendation:** Fireflies meeting→project tagging, research-paper study-design classification, and spring exit-note trajectory scoring survived triage; only the Fireflies tagger satisfies all three conditions, and it was the recommendation.
- **Explicit rejections with reasons:** the Tech Inventory athlete-data flag (Jev sees only a brand name; a 09-29 run is already chartered), matchup injury triage (fetching is code, not judgment), Ath_Medicine themes / CATES grading (surgery probe failed and clinical-text egress is a user-level decision), and rerank / evidence tags / `sde_cascade` (already measured and dropped in the prior sweep).
- **"Maintenance" is an allowed answer:** given ~3 meetings/week, even the recommended win is modest. Stopping at maintenance — keep the router and verifier, stop hunting for new Jev applications — was flagged as the sandbox's own recorded advice and remained on the table.
- **Nothing was built.** The session ended at a recommendation with a pre-registered pass bar, awaiting an explicit user pick of one option or none.

## Details

The three conditions function as a filter against the most common failure mode in LLM adoption: applying a model to work that deterministic code already does correctly and cheaply. Condition (1) screens out tasks whose apparent difficulty is really a schema problem — lookups, joins, and threshold comparisons are code. Condition (2) screens out speculative capability: if no existing consumer reads the output, the model's answer has no place to land and the build produces an artifact nobody uses. Condition (3) is the strictest and the one that eliminated most candidates, because it demands a *measured* shortfall of plain code, not an assumed one. The sweep's value came largely from producing those measurements (see [[concepts/fireflies-meeting-project-tagging]] for the numbers that cleared condition 3 for the recommended candidate), and from discovering that for the research-classification candidate the honest baseline had never actually been run.

The rejections are as informative as the survivors. The Tech Inventory flag fails condition (1) because the model's entire input is a vendor brand name — a lookup table's job. Matchup injury triage fails the same condition: the hard part is fetching data, and fetching is code. The Ath_Medicine themes and CATES grading candidates were blocked at a different layer entirely — a surgery probe had already failed, and whether clinical text may be sent to an external model is a governance decision reserved to the user, not an engineering trade-off (the same data-sensitivity boundary that governs the anonymization rules in [[concepts/ath-medicine-project]]). The rerank, evidence-tag, and `sde_cascade` ideas were not re-litigated because the prior sweep had already measured and dropped them, which is the sweep's own discipline applied recursively: a measured negative result is durable and should not be re-opened without new evidence. Finally, the sweep explicitly priced the recommended win against its base rate — ~3 meetings per week — and concluded the honest ceiling was modest, which is why "do nothing beyond maintenance" was preserved as a legitimate terminal option rather than treated as failure to find work.

# DEV Project Migration to GitHub + Google Drive (Destination-Split Policy)

On 2026-09-14, a staged full-DEV migration moved all Codex and Claude projects to durable remote storage, governed by a destination-split policy that routes each artifact type to GitHub, Google Drive, or neither based on sensitivity and size. The audit at migration start counted 142 local repos with `erash11` remotes, 144 GitHub repos (141 private / 3 public), and none ahead of remote; Google Drive was mounted at `G:\My Drive` with `_DRIVE` mapping to `00_Primary_Storage_Drive`. On 2026-09-24 the policy entered an operational phase: the S2 evaluation data was migrated to Drive and a Parquet-snapshot exchange layer was stood up so two machines could share data without reaching into each other's live working trees.

## Key Points

- **Destination split by artifact type:** code / docs / `AGENTS.md` / `STATUS.md` → GitHub; large datasets, vendor exports, installers, and proprietary files → Google Drive; athlete-identifiable or health data → Drive only (never GitHub); raw conversation transcripts → Drive backup (never in project repos); credentials and `.env` files → neither destination; sanitized memory and handoff summaries → private GitHub context repos.
- **Working repos stay local:** live Git working directories remain under `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV`. Google Drive holds external data and archives, not live working repos.
- **Intentional public/local exceptions:** `Travel_Map`, `SportScienceResearchRepo`, and `JumpReporting` remain intentionally public; `DexaProject` stays local/Drive-only due to sensitive athlete data and is never pushed to GitHub.
- **Codex history not durably backed up:** Codex conversation history is preserved locally under `C:\Users\eric_rash\.codex\sessions\` but is NOT in GitHub and NOT independently backed up off-device — a remaining gap.
- **Raw backups are themselves sensitive:** raw conversation backups contain athlete names, medical context, and historical credentials, so the Drive archive must stay private and unshared — the backup inherits the sensitivity of the most sensitive content it captures.
- **Snapshot exchange, not live cross-reads (2026-09-24):** each pull repo runs `export_snapshot.py` to emit Parquet snapshots that the other machine consumes; the Mac rsyncs `ol_scores.csv` and `team_scores.csv` from `~/DEV/S2_Evaluation/data/` into the Drive S2 folder, and Perch's Windows reads are queued to be repointed at the snapshots rather than at live sources.
- **The Drive-only rule is enforced at the tool layer, and that costs verifiability (2026-09-24):** a direct listing of the S2 Drive folder was refused because the listing itself contains an athlete-named file, leaving the migration's arrival unconfirmed rather than verified.

## Details

The migration's governing principle is that destination is a function of both size and sensitivity, not a single default. Ordinary code and documentation flow to GitHub where version history and collaboration matter; bulky or proprietary binaries (datasets, vendor exports, installers) go to Google Drive to keep repositories lean; and anything athlete-identifiable or health-related is confined to Drive-only storage so it never enters a Git remote at all. Credentials and `.env` files are excluded from both remotes entirely. Sanitized memory and handoff summaries occupy a fourth lane — private GitHub "context repos" — allowing durable, version-controlled continuity documents without exposing raw sensitive material. This mirrors the athlete-data-stays-local convention already established in Baylor's sports-tech pipelines (see [[concepts/kinexon-volleyball-tracking-project]] and [[concepts/speedprofiling-velocity-project]]), where `data/` directories are gitignored so athlete-level data never leaves the machine.

Seven remaining Claude Cowork projects (S2 Cognition, WebApps, PlayerProfiles, StaffProject_BE, Post Season Analysis, UPskilling, PersonalKnowledgeManagement) were queued for migration via a `/migrate-project-to-disk` command and later reported complete in a resume checkpoint pending verification. Several follow-ups remained open: confirming that `Ath_Medicine`, `Baylor_Exposure_Data`, and `Risk_Stratification_Engine` contain no identifiable athlete/health data before their GitHub state is trusted; resolving `_INBOX` changes (a modified `recv.py`, two untracked closeout scripts, and five recovered Python utilities from `agent-skills/_recovered-from-codex/`); a guarded Windows skills v2 sync blocked on an absent `.sync-v2-ready` marker with divergent agent/Codex skill copies to reconcile; and stale documentation (`_INBOX/docs/STATUS.md` still claiming 7 Cowork projects remain, and a stale root "36 `.from-windows` files" item). Optional cleanup included removing a 3.2 GB `C:\Users\eric_rash\Documents\Codex` scratch folder and duplicate clones under `Desktop\DEV\_to_delete\2026-09-14_dup_clones`. Key final commits: DEV router `847bfb9`, `_INBOX` migration handoff `c7e0326`, Claude config `9e807eb`, global memory `b59bf55`, recovered agent utilities `4e00e86`.

The 2026-09-24 machine-split day exercised the policy in two instructive ways. First, once data lives on Drive rather than in a repo, two machines working the same projects need a defined exchange format; the answer adopted was per-repo `export_snapshot.py` runs producing Parquet snapshots, with each host reading the committed snapshot instead of the other host's live data — a read-only, reproducible handoff that keeps the Drive copy authoritative and avoids the divergence problems that plague direct cross-machine reads. Second, the Drive-only rule for athlete data proved to be enforced mechanically and more broadly than the written policy suggests: the permission layer refused a mere *directory listing* of the S2 folder because athlete names appear in file names, meaning identifiable data lives in the metadata as well as the payload (see [[concepts/athlete-data-permission-block]]). No workaround was attempted, so the cost was accepted as an explicit verification gap in the day's handoff — the guardrail behaving correctly, at the price of not being able to confirm from that session that the migration landed.

# Do-Not-Send Gate on Audited Deliverables

A do-not-send gate is an explicit, recorded hold placed on a finished-looking deliverable after an audit finds defects that would mislead its audience. On 2026-09-18 the TOS evidence brief was placed under such a gate: the decision was written into working memory rather than left as conversational context, an enumerated fix list was attached as the release condition, and the hold was propagated to a downstream artifact ("Research in 5 #002 (TOS)", built with PR #8 open) that depended on the same uncorrected numbers.

## Key Points

- **The gate is recorded, not remembered.** The do-not-send decision was written to working memory so it survives session boundaries — a finished-looking artifact is otherwise likely to be sent by default later.
- **The gate carries an explicit release condition.** The hold names exactly what must be fixed (three misquotes, the Poisson argument, the order-of-magnitude figure, the source-count claim, the NCAA source-dating, and the over-strong recommendation language), converting "don't send" from a vague misgiving into a closeable checklist.
- **Holds propagate to dependents.** The Research in 5 #002 deliverable was built and had an open PR but was explicitly marked NOT sent, "gated on the same fixes" — a downstream artifact inherits the defects of the numbers it reuses.
- **Risk tiering replaces a binary verdict.** Rather than pass/fail, the audit graded reliance: high risk for causal/comparative/policy use, moderate for the staff-education one-pagers, lower for the long-form review as a source map. This keeps partially-valid work usable for the purposes it can support.
- **"Built and PR-open" is not "ready."** Completion of the production pipeline is orthogonal to correctness of content; the gate sits between them.

## Details

The failure mode a do-not-send gate guards against is specific: an artifact that is complete, formatted, and visibly finished exerts pressure toward release, and any unrecorded reservation about its content erodes over days until someone forwards it. Writing the hold into working memory makes the reservation durable and makes it the first thing a future session encounters when the artifact resurfaces. Attaching an enumerated fix list serves a second purpose — it defines what would *lift* the gate, so the hold is not an open-ended veto but a tracked state with a known exit. Without that list, holds tend to resolve in one of two bad ways: the artifact is quietly abandoned despite most of it being sound, or it is released after a vague "I think we addressed that."

Propagation is the part most easily missed. The Research in 5 #002 piece was a separate, independently completed deliverable with its own open pull request, and nothing about its own build process indicated a problem — its defects were inherited entirely from reusing the brief's numbers. Any hold on a source document must therefore be traced to every artifact that consumed its figures, which in this case also meant the working review, the full PDF, the briefing note, and the one-pagers. The accompanying reliance tiering is what keeps the gate proportionate: the long-form review remained usable as a source map even while the brief was blocked from distribution, because the audit separated "which claims are unsupported" from "which uses depend on those claims." That separation lets legitimate work continue during remediation instead of discarding the whole artifact set.

# Pre-Registered Pass Bar Before a Model Run

A pre-registered pass bar is an accuracy threshold, a coverage requirement, and a test set defined and recorded *before* any model is run against the task. On 2026-09-22 this was applied to the recommended Jev candidate: ≥90% precision when the model is confident, confidence on ≥60% of meetings, measured against ~40 hand-tagged meetings from July onward. The hand-tagging was made a prerequisite of proceeding, not a step to be improvised after seeing results.

## Key Points

- **Two-part bar, precision and coverage:** ≥90% precision *conditional on the model being confident*, plus confidence on ≥60% of items. Precision alone is gameable by an abstaining model; coverage alone is gameable by a reckless one.
- **Test set specified in advance:** ~40 meetings hand-tagged by the user, drawn from July onward, produced *before* any Jev call — so the labels cannot be influenced by seeing model output.
- **Written down before the run, not after.** The bar was recorded as part of the recommendation, making it a commitment rather than a post-hoc rationalization of whatever number appeared.
- **A ready-made labeled set is not automatically a fair test.** The research-classification candidate had 197 human `studyDesign` labels available, yet was still held back because the *baseline* it would be compared against had never been run.
- **Some candidates cannot meet any bar and should be judged on other grounds.** Spring exit-note scoring (n=34) was acknowledged as unable to demonstrate accuracy; its stated payoff is reproducibility, not a threshold.

## Details

The two-part structure of the bar exists because either half alone can be satisfied trivially. A model that declares confidence on two easy items and abstains on the rest achieves perfect conditional precision while doing nothing useful; a model forced to answer everything achieves full coverage at unusable precision. Requiring ≥90% precision *when confident* together with confidence on ≥60% of items forces the confidence signal itself to be calibrated — the model must know which meetings it can read and say so. This pairs directly with the candidate's abstention fallback (`project: unfiled`), which makes the 40% non-confident remainder harmless rather than wrong; the bar and the fallback design are the same decision viewed from two sides.

Specifying the test set in advance closes the more subtle loophole. Labels created after seeing model output drift toward the model's reading of ambiguous cases, which is precisely the population the evaluation is supposed to adjudicate. Requiring ~40 hand-tagged meetings *before any Jev call* makes the labels independent of the system under test — the same out-of-sample discipline that the Wednesday freeze-capture enforces for a forecasting model, where the only trustworthy grade comes from predictions frozen before outcomes exist. The research-classification case shows the discipline's second edge: possessing 197 human `studyDesign` labels plus INCLUDE/EXCLUDE decisions looks like a solved evaluation problem, but a test set is only half of a comparison. Without a fairly-specified baseline — first-page-text regex, not the title-only regex that already fails on 80 of 197 — a passing score would prove only that the model beats a deliberately weak opponent. Finally, the spring exit-note candidate demonstrates honest handling of a task where no bar is reachable: at n=34, with a prior Claude one-off pass at ρ=+0.30 against PFF snaps and a keyword rubric scoring zero on 51% of notes, the project was reframed around reproducibility next spring and around hand-set (not fitted) weights, because fitting on 34 players would overfit.

# Connection: Agreement Between Two Independent Extractions as the Verification Method

## The Connection

Three sessions in this knowledge base verify machine-derived content not by inspecting it more carefully but by obtaining a *second, independently produced* version of the same content and diffing the two. On 2026-09-25, course-video transcripts were checked by comparing a locally generated ASR pass against the site-provided player captions, with the comparison report itself as an artifact ([[concepts/course-video-transcript-verification-pipeline]]). On 2026-04-22, a background agent's citation fixes were checked by extracting the PDF text with PyPDF2 and reading the actual author lists, which exposed three hallucinated citations ([[concepts/sportscience-research-repo-batch-import]]). On 2026-06-25, the trustworthiness of local Fireflies search was established by comparing the local cache's transcript count against the live API's (0 vs. 196), which revealed a silent desync ([[concepts/fireflies-cli-name-search-vault-ingest]]).

## Key Insight

The distinguishing move is not "check against ground truth" but "obtain two derivations with uncorrelated error profiles and let their disagreement localize the uncertainty." This is strictly more informative than a single careful read, because it produces a *map* of where the content is unreliable rather than a binary judgment about the whole artifact. ASR and vendor captions fail on different words; an LLM summarizing a paper and a byte-level PDF text extraction fail on different fields; a stale local cache and a live API disagree precisely where the cache is wrong.

The corollary is that the residue of agreement is what earns trust, and the residue of disagreement must be surfaced rather than silently resolved. The Part 3 transcript's one unclear injury term is the honest output of this method: the two sources disagreed, neither settled it, and the term was flagged with the absence of a manual audio review recorded alongside it — rather than one source being arbitrarily preferred to make the artifact look finished. The same discipline distinguishes the citation repair (three specific IDs corrected before commit) from a blanket "reviewed" claim. Where only one derivation is available, the fallback is not confidence but an explicit draft label, which is why the 2026-09-24 machine transcript was marked as needing cleanup before staff-facing use ([[concepts/wistia-course-video-extraction]]).

A practical selection rule follows: when building a verification step, look for a second source that already exists and is cheap to obtain — vendor captions shipped with the video, the raw PDF behind an agent's summary, the live API behind a local cache — before designing a bespoke review process. The second source is usually already sitting there unused.

## Evidence

- 2026-09-25 (10:19): "Dual-transcript verification (yt-dlp/ASR vs. player captions + comparison report) is the accepted workflow for this course"; Part 3 retained "one unclear injury term flagged in the transcript; no manual audio review was done."
- 2026-04-22 (10:57): a background repair agent hallucinated author lists for IDs 286, 287, 358; "Used PyPDF2 text extraction to verify actual authors and corrected all three citations before committing."
- 2026-06-25 (13:34): local Fireflies cache held 0 transcripts against the live API's 196, so local search would have silently returned nothing until a full resync was performed.

# End-of-Day Structured Interview Workflow

A structured end-of-day interview workflow was demonstrated on 2026-05-29, combining a Fireflies meeting sync, a 4-question daily debrief, targeted vault note creation, and global memory system updates (USER.md and MEMORY.md). The session also revealed a critical USER.md character cap constraint and clarified the Tier A vs. Tier B memory split for active vs. durable information.

## Key Points

- **4-question interview format** covers all active projects and workstreams in a single pass, surfacing insights across areas that might otherwise receive no end-of-day attention. The 2026-05-29 run spanned: Dropback vendor call, Jeremy presentation prep, Hoff/Soto AI discovery call, ACWR tennis project, Fall Camp simulator scoping, spirit and cheer summer packet, research database, and upcoming Databricks call.
- **Q4 ("tell a peer one thing") consistently produces the sharpest material:** this prompt forces compression — the user must identify the single transmissible insight from the day. On 2026-05-29 it surfaced: "effort put into answering questions that haven't been asked is in vain" (essay seed), and the connected observation that AI adoption/consensus is the real bottleneck, not direction.
- **Connect interview outputs to existing vault notes rather than creating isolated ones:** updating the existing `self-authored-direction` note with a reframed open question (linking direction to adoption) compounds value more than creating a standalone new note. The connection is the knowledge, not just the content.
- **USER.md cap (1,375 chars):** the global USER.md profile is essentially at capacity (1,370/1,375 as of 2026-05-29). Any future profile addition requires consolidating or pruning existing entries before adding new content — USER.md must be treated as a fixed-size buffer, not an append-only log.
- **MEMORY.md Tier A vs. Tier B:** durable facts about the user go in Tier A; active, fluid threads (e.g., career-pivot consideration) go in Tier B. A Tier B entry signals "this is worth tracking but not yet stable enough to become a fact."
- **Fireflies integration:** new meetings are synced, renamed from generic timestamps to descriptive titles (e.g., `2026-05-28_Eric_and_Jeremy_presentation_prep`), and exported to the vault at `Inbox/meetings/YYYY-MM-DD_<title>.md`.

## Details

The structured end-of-day interview functions as a compression mechanism: a full day of meetings, decisions, and half-formed thoughts is distilled into a small set of high-signal outputs — a vault note, a memory update, an essay seed — without requiring the user to decide in the moment what is worth capturing. By following a fixed question format, the interview ensures consistent coverage across all active workstreams rather than capturing only what was most recent or most emotionally salient. The structure also makes the interview reproducible across sessions and assistants: the same prompt set can be run by any AI instance with access to the user's project context and yield comparable coverage.

The Q4 prompt is architecturally different from the preceding questions because it forces a different cognitive operation. Questions 1–3 surface facts and status updates (what happened, what decisions were made, what is blocked); Q4 forces synthesis and compression — the user must identify the single insight worth transmitting to a peer. This compression step often reveals insights that would not have surfaced through status-update prompts alone. On 2026-05-29, both outputs from Q4 were routed to vault notes rather than MEMORY.md, because they are essay seeds and framing questions rather than durable facts about the user's preferences or context. The distinction matters: MEMORY.md stores facts that help a future AI session orient quickly ("user works at Baylor Athletics"), while vault notes store ideas that the user may want to develop, publish, or return to. AI-adoption/consensus was explicitly deferred to the weekly review rather than drafted immediately — the weekly review is the right context for framing the evidence, finding allies, and deciding whether the idea is worth writing.

# SpeedProfiling GPS–Play-by-Play Alignment and On-Field Separation (Ticket 05)

Ticket 05 of the SpeedProfiling project merged 10 Hz Catapult GPS data with college football play-by-play, separated on-field athletes from sideline/bench players, and produced per-play workload tables. On 2026-07-20 the ticket was closed after resolving a kickoff-offset misalignment, replacing unusable venue metadata with a PCA-recovered field frame, and adopting a two-part on-field rule. The ticket shipped on PR #3 (taken out of draft) with offset `-15` committed as `b22401b`.

## Key Points

- **Kickoff surge signature as a numerical time anchor:** the kickoff is the only game moment when 6+ athletes exceed ~10 mph in the same second, making it a reliable signature for aligning GPS timestamps to play-by-play across games. Script 02 scans ±3 minutes for this signature, centers the animation viewport on the located kickoff, hides non-moving bench dots, and colors dots by speed.
- **Alignment stays manual per spec:** the script prints a *suggested* offset (`TIMESTAMP_OFFSET_SEC`) but never sets it. Eric set `-15` after the play-by-play's estimated t=0 was found to lag the true kickoff by ~13 s; the re-run re-detected the surge at t≈+2 (within ±3 s tolerance) and tightened participation to 10.8 athletes/play.
- **Windows open ~2 s before the break by design (`SURGE_BREAK_LEAD_SEC`):** the sweep starting at t≈1.5–2 s rather than exactly 0 is intentional — windows must open before players break so ticket 06 sprint qualification can capture the below-0.5 mph standstill before acceleration. Windows opening *after* the break is the bad direction.
- **Venue metadata was a dead end:** the activity's venue is the Baylor *practice field*, so raw X/Y arrived ~600 m off-stadium at unknown rotation. PCA on in-play fast-moving samples recovers the field frame instead of relying on venue coordinates.
- **Two-part on-field rule:** the team box straddles the calibrated sideline, so a boundary rule alone counted 46 athletes/play. Adding a metabolic-power gate (mean M ≥ 3 W/kg) brings the median to ~10 (≈11 expected). This is a documented method deviation.
- **GPS spike rows (>25 mph) are excluded** from both max-velocity and distance sums.

## Details

The core alignment problem was that the play-by-play's estimated kickoff time (t=0) was not the actual kickoff instant — it trailed the real event by roughly 13 seconds. The original `kickoff_alignment.gif`, windowed from t=−5 to +20, therefore showed the tail of the coverage sprint plus post-touchback milling rather than the clean "wave running down the field." Eric's report that he could only see players "waffling about" outside the boundary with a faint, indistinct surge was accurate feedback about the misalignment, not a perception failure. The resolution had two parts: setting `TIMESTAMP_OFFSET_SEC <- -15` to shift GPS into agreement with play-by-play, and — more durably — reworking the animation tooling so the kickoff is localized *numerically* (scanning ±3 min for the surge signature) and the viewport is centered on it, with bench dots hidden and dots colored by speed. This embodies the lesson that when a visual-judgment aid fails to give a judgeable signal, the fix is to the tooling/viewport, not to ask the human to look harder.

Two field-geometry and roster challenges were also resolved. The Catapult activity's venue metadata pointed at the Baylor practice field, so raw coordinates landed ~600 m from the stadium at unknown rotation and could not be used to establish field bounds — a dead end that was replaced by running PCA on fast-moving in-play GPS samples to recover the field's coordinate frame. Separating the ~11 on-field athletes from the full squad required more than a sideline-boundary test, because the team box straddles the calibrated sideline: the boundary rule alone over-counted at 46 athletes/play. Adding a metabolic-power gate (mean metabolic power ≥ 3 W/kg) filtered to genuinely active players, producing a median of ~10 on-field athletes against ~11 expected, and was recorded as a documented method deviation. Spike rows above 25 mph were excluded from both max-velocity and distance calculations to prevent GPS artifacts from corrupting workload sums. Ticket 05 closed with all five checkboxes complete and PR #3 moved out of draft; the stacked-PR merge order remains #1 → #2 → #3.

# Flush Selective Retention on Non-Working Sessions

The memory-compiler flush stage normally emits `FLUSH_OK` — writing nothing to the daily log — when a session produced no durable knowledge. The 2026-08-05 flush demonstrates a middle case: a session that was explicitly "a data snapshot, not a working session," with no decisions and no lessons, but whose contents were nonetheless preserved because several items carried hard deadlines or closing windows. The flush wrote the items down *and* annotated why, making the retention decision auditable rather than implicit.

## Key Points

- **Two distinct retention criteria.** The default criterion is *knowledge durability* (did this session teach something reusable?). The 2026-08-05 flush applied a second, orthogonal criterion: *time sensitivity* (will this item expire or escalate if not surfaced?). An item can fail the first test and still pass the second.
- **The retention rationale was written into the log itself.** The flush appended an explicit note — "This was a data snapshot, not a working session — no decisions or lessons produced. The action items above are preserved only because several are time-sensitive" — so a downstream reader (or compiler) knows the entry is a deliberate exception, not a misclassification.
- **Non-decision content is labeled as such.** The action items were headed "surfaced for follow-up, not new decisions," preventing the compiler from later mistaking a triage snapshot for a decision record.
- **What qualified as time-sensitive:** a security alert, a counterparty's closing availability window (leave dates), and immediate signature/confirmation actions. Ordinary aging replies were included only as context around these.
- **Cost trade-off:** preserving a snapshot costs a small amount of daily-log volume; discarding one risks dropping a deadline entirely, since the snapshot has no other durable home once the session ends.

## Details

The flush stage sits at a lossy boundary: it reads a session transcript and decides what, if anything, survives into `daily/YYYY-MM-DD.md`. Its default posture is aggressive discard, because most session chatter is transient and the daily logs are the compiler's source of truth. But a purely knowledge-oriented filter has a blind spot — operational obligations. A triage snapshot contains no lesson, no decision, and no reusable pattern, so it fails a strict "durable knowledge" test, yet it may be the only artifact in the system holding a 3-day-old security alert or a leave window that closes in three days. Once the session closes and the transcript is archived, that obligation has no other retrieval path.

The 2026-08-05 flush resolved this by widening the retention test rather than relaxing it: the items were kept under an explicitly named second criterion, and the reasoning was recorded inline. This self-documenting exception is the transferable practice. It avoids two failure modes at once — silently dropping deadline-bearing content, and silently inflating the log with snapshots that a future reader would mistake for substantive work. The pattern parallels the triage-vs-execution split seen in the inbox-triage runs themselves: surfacing and categorizing is a distinct act from deciding, and labeling output as one or the other keeps the downstream consumer honest. It also complements the broader principle behind the on-ramp pipeline — keep material retrievable while keeping the standing context lean — by admitting only the subset whose expiry cost justifies the space.

# Project Triage and Retrospective Methodology

On 2026-05-21, a structured 7-day retrospective (covering May 14–21) and a cold-project triage exercise were conducted to address project sprawl across many concurrent initiatives. The retrospective produced a structured cross-project summary of work completed and 7 open loops with next actions; the triage sorted cold projects into 4 buckets and shipped a decision-tracking HTML artifact at `Desktop/DEV/cold-projects-triage.html`.

## Key Points

- **7-day retrospective format:** a structured recap of all projects touched in a rolling window, categorized by status, covering CLI development (Zotero, Catapult), 5 new skills installed, Fireflies setup, memory and Obsidian integration, token dashboard setup, and side fixes for May 14–21. Concluded with 7 identified open loops, each paired with a concrete next action.

The 2026-05-21 run sorted 16 projects: 3 resume, 2 decide, 3 done, 8 archive/kill.

The retrospective was triggered by the user explicitly losing track of what had been started, stopped, or left mid-flight — a common failure mode when many parallel workstreams run simultaneously across different tools, repositories, and roles. Rather than relying on memory or ad-hoc review, the session generated a structured cross-project summary covering the prior 7 days, making the "what exists and where it stands" question answerable in a single, deliberate pass. The format mirrors a lightweight sprint retrospective: scope (what was touched), status (done vs. in-flight vs. blocked), and open loops (concrete next actions, not vague intentions).

The 4-bucket triage model is designed to force explicit decisions rather than letting cold projects accumulate indefinitely in an ambiguous "maybe later" state. **Resume** identifies projects with a clear next action that are still worth pursuing. **Decide** surfaces projects that need a deliberate go/no-go call rather than being quietly ignored — the act of naming these forces a decision that passive neglect defers indefinitely. **Done** provides a formal closure signal for work that is genuinely complete but hasn't been officially closed. **Archive/Kill** handles deliberate deprioritization — not forgotten, but explicitly moved out of active consideration. The HTML artifact makes the triage durable and reviewable without accessing the session that produced it; sharing it as a file also separates the "what was triaged" question from the "what should I do next" question, allowing the artifact to be reviewed asynchronously.

The retrospective also surfaced a secondary benefit: completing deferred follow-up work from prior sessions. Specifically, the Zotero CLI's `sync --full` verification — left pending after the v0.1 slash command was registered on 2026-05-19 — was completed during the retrospective, with 2,064 items ingested successfully in ~75 seconds. Catching and completing loose ends like this is a natural output of a structured retrospective: open loops that were "almost done" become clearly visible and easy to close within the retrospective session itself.

# Connection: Verify Directly, Don't Trust the Intermediate Layer

## The Connection

Both substantive sessions on 2026-04-22 ran into a version of the same problem: a tool or agent produced output that *looked* fine - a citation with a plausible author list, a photo wired into HTML with a correct relative path - but was actually wrong or unverifiable through the usual checking method. In [[concepts/sportscience-research-repo-batch-import]], a background repair agent's citation fixes for IDs 286, 287, and 358 contained hallucinated author lists despite correctly identifying the papers' topics. In [[concepts/the-monitor-newsletter]], Blake Wright's photo failed to appear in the localhost preview server even though the HTML and file path were both correct.

## Key Insight

In both cases, the fix was not to redo the original work but to change the *verification method* to something closer to the ground truth. The hallucinated citations were caught by extracting the actual PDF text with PyPDF2 and reading it directly, rather than trusting the agent's summarized output. The "broken" photo was confirmed to be fine by opening the HTML file directly in Chrome via `file://`, rather than trusting the brainstorm preview server's rendering. The shared lesson: when an agent, tool, or service produces output that looks plausible but can't be easily double-checked through the same channel, step down to a more primitive, lower-level check (raw file text, direct file rendering) before accepting the result as correct.

## Evidence

- 2026-04-22 (10:57): "Background agent produced `docs/batch_r7_fixes.json` but hallucinated wrong author lists for IDs 286, 287, and 358... Used PyPDF2 text extraction to verify actual authors and corrected all three citations before committing."
- 2026-04-22 (17:21): "Photo failed to render in localhost preview — identified as a server limitation (brainstorm preview server doesn't serve image files), not an HTML error... always verify photo rendering by opening the HTML directly in Chrome via file:// URL."

# Claude Code Three-Tier Memory Architecture

The Claude Code memory system is composed of three independent layers, each operating at a different granularity and owned by a different mechanism. This architecture was articulated on 2026-05-19 during a session that traced exactly when and how each capture mechanism fires, and clarified several non-obvious details about hook timing and agent visibility. On 2026-06-05, a practical capacity-management routing pattern emerged for when Tier B global memory approaches its character cap.

## Key Points

- **Tier A — Native Claude Code auto-memory:** Built into Claude Code itself; managed per-project; no user configuration required. Operates automatically within a project context; its exact retention and synthesis mechanics are not user-visible.
- **Tier B — Custom global scratchpad via Stop hook:** A user-configured hook on the `Stop` event, which fires after every conversation turn. This provides incremental, per-turn transcript capture to a global scratchpad file (MEMORY.md) — a granularity that neither Tier A nor Tier C provides.
- **Tier C — claude-memory-compiler:** The [[concepts/claude-memory-compiler-setup]] system: `SessionEnd` and `PreCompact` hooks fire shell commands at session teardown or auto-compaction, spawning a detached `flush.py` process that appends structured notes to the daily log; at end-of-day these are compiled into knowledge articles.
- **The agent never sees a "session ending" event.** Session end and compaction are harness-level events; it is the Claude Code harness that runs the hook shell commands, not the agent itself. This means an in-context agent cannot intercept or react to its own termination — only the hooks can.
- **PreCompact as a safety net:** In a long session with multiple auto-compactions, PreCompact fires before each one. If a session later crashes before `SessionEnd` fires, at least one Tier C log was written at the most recent compaction — preventing total context loss.
- **When Tier B is near cap, route to Tier A project files:** The global MEMORY.md (Tier B) has a character-cap constraint. When it approaches capacity, new durable facts should be saved to Tier A project-specific memory files (e.g., `project_<name>.md`, `user_career_timeline.md`) rather than forcing compression of existing Tier B entries. Tier A project files are cross-project searchable via memsearch — they are not siloed to a single project context.

## Details

The three tiers are designed to capture context at different time horizons and granularities, and they operate independently rather than hierarchically. Tier A is fully opaque to the user — Claude Code manages it internally on a per-project basis. Tier B's Stop-hook scratchpad is the most granular: because the Stop event fires after every conversation turn, Tier B can capture mid-session context incrementally in near-real-time. This is especially useful for long sessions where intermediate turns might be compacted away before Tier C's end-of-session capture fires. Tier C produces the richest synthesized output — compiled knowledge articles from daily logs — but fires only at session boundaries.

The independence of the three tiers is their key reliability property. A failure in one does not cascade to the others: if a session crashes before `SessionEnd` fires (blocking Tier C's flush), the Stop-hook's Tier B scratchpad may still contain the session's important turns. If the Stop hook misfires, Tier A's native memory and Tier C's PreCompact-triggered captures are unaffected. The "agent never sees session ending" detail is architecturally important for anyone building on top of these hooks: code written inside the agent context cannot detect or react to its own session ending. Teardown logic must be placed in hook shell commands that the harness executes, not in agent-side instructions. This distinction separates what the LLM can do (respond to turns, use tools) from what the harness can do (run shell commands on system events like session end, compaction, or turn completion).

The Tier B near-cap routing pattern (2026-06-05) addresses a practical capacity constraint that emerges over time as the global MEMORY.md accumulates active threads. The USER.md profile has a hard 1,375-character cap (documented in [[concepts/end-of-day-structured-interview]]), and MEMORY.md's Tier B can similarly fill as a productive user's open questions and active threads accumulate across weeks. The correct response when Tier B is near capacity is not to compress existing entries — which risks discarding information encoded in current phrasing — but to route new durable facts into named Tier A project memory files. These files are typically named per relationship or project (e.g., `project_kenny_boyd.md` for facts about a key stakeholder, `user_career_timeline.md` for career-context facts that help future sessions orient quickly) but are surfaced by memsearch across all project contexts. Routing to Tier A therefore sacrifices no cross-project retrievability while relieving pressure on the shared Tier B capacity. Facts that belong in Tier A project files are those that are both durable (will not become stale quickly) and specific enough that they do not need to live in the global scope — as opposed to cross-cutting facts about user preferences or universal workflow patterns that genuinely belong in Tier B's global scope.

# Fireflies Meeting→Project Tagging (Jev Candidate #1)

Meeting→project tagging assigns each Fireflies meeting a chartered-project tag so downstream workflows can group meetings by project instead of sorting them by hand. On 2026-09-22 it was identified as the only Jev (System One model) candidate satisfying all three of the leverage sweep's admission conditions, on the strength of measured failure rates for every deterministic approach tried. It was recommended but not built; the session closed awaiting a user pick.

## Key Points

- **Every plain-code approach was measured and failed.** The exact project name appears in **0 of 279** meetings. Naive word matching hits 252 meetings but **210 of those are ambiguous** across multiple projects. Attendee lookup resolves only **6%** (18 of 279).
- **"None of these" must be a valid output.** Of the 84 meetings with named speakers, **39 map to no chartered project** — a classifier forced to choose among known projects would mislabel roughly half of its resolvable cases.
- **Two existing consumers already need the tag.** `status-report` carries no project tag on meetings at all, so the drafting pass re-sorts them by hand every run; `meeting-prep` step 2 searches vault notes for the literal project name, which the 0-of-279 figure shows cannot work.
- **Failure is free.** The low-confidence fallback is `project: unfiled` — byte-identical to today's behavior — so an abstaining classifier costs nothing relative to the status quo.
- **The win is reuse, not reasoning:** the value is a tag written once and read many times downstream, not novel inference per meeting. At ~3 meetings/week the absolute payoff is modest.

## Details

The candidate clears the sweep's third and strictest condition — plain code tried first and measurably short — more cleanly than anything else surveyed (see [[concepts/jev-leverage-sweep-typesafe]]). The three measurements are complementary rather than redundant: exact-name matching fails on *recall* (0/279, because people do not say the chartered project name in meetings), naive word matching fails on *precision* (252 hits but 210 ambiguous across projects), and attendee lookup fails on *coverage* (6%, because attendance does not determine subject). Together they close off the deterministic design space rather than leaving an untried alternative, which is exactly the evidentiary standard the research-classification candidate could not meet — there, a fair first-page regex baseline had never been run.

The "39 of 84 map to no chartered project" figure is the design-critical finding. It means the output space is not the set of chartered projects but that set plus an explicit null, and that a classifier evaluated only on its ability to pick the right project among known options would look good while being wrong on a large fraction of real inputs. Pairing that null option with the `project: unfiled` fallback produces a favorable risk profile: the system's worst case reproduces present behavior exactly, so the only way the build loses is the cost of building it. The consumers justify that cost more than the per-meeting reasoning does — `status-report`'s hand-sorting is repeated work eliminated once per drafting pass, and `meeting-prep` step 2's literal-name vault search is provably broken by the 0-of-279 result. Both are instances of the broader Fireflies-corpus hygiene problem that descriptive renaming also addresses: metadata written once at ingest makes every downstream retrieval cheaper.

# ForcePlate_DecisionSystem: Metric Reliability and Classifier Recalibration

ForcePlate_DecisionSystem is a Baylor Athletics project for force-plate measurement and readiness-classification. On 2026-07-22, it was advanced as one of two shippable tracks that emerged after a grilled "Practice → Saturday transfer" observational study design was killed (Baylor's practice load is too standardized to support the design). The session produced a measurement-reliability analysis of CMJ and IMTP metrics, a recalibration of the single-test readiness classifier, and a time-critical testing recommendation for Camp 2026, all left as a clean, pushed, green draft PR (#1) with the merge decision deferred to the user.

## Key Points

- **No CMJ metric resolves the smallest worthwhile change at weekly cadence:** 0 of 10 CMJ force-plate metrics have a typical error (TE) small enough to resolve the smallest worthwhile change (SWC) when tested weekly — week-to-week noise swamps real change.
- **RSI-modified is a poor lead metric:** RSI-modified (mRSI), the field-default readiness metric, is the 2nd-noisiest of the 10 CMJ metrics (8.8% TE) versus 3.8% TE for Peak Power/BM — arguing against leading readiness monitoring with mRSI.
- **IMTP moved to 4×/season:** IMTP week-to-week noise (13%) exceeds its real 3–6-month change (11%), so testing more often than the real signal moves is wasteful; IMTP was recalibrated to 4×/season and documented in the Camp 2026 testing ask.
- **Single-test classifier ladder recalibrated:** the readiness classifier's single-test threshold ladder (>30 red / >25 orange / >15 yellow) was recalibrated to match the consecutive-test ladder; 281 of 1,640 reds reclassified, all from the single-test path.
- **Deferred production re-run:** re-running the 10,592 existing classified rows to pick up the recalibrated flags mutates production data and was deferred to the user's timing call, after the ForcePlate PR merges.

## Details

The reliability analysis reframes how force-plate data should drive readiness decisions. A metric is only useful for detecting change if its measurement noise (typical error) is smaller than the change worth acting on (the smallest worthwhile change). At weekly cadence none of the 10 CMJ metrics clear that bar, which means week-to-week readiness swings read largely as noise rather than signal. The practical consequence is twofold: readiness monitoring should not lead with RSI-modified (the field default and 2nd-noisiest metric at 8.8% TE), and lower-noise metrics such as Peak Power/BM (3.8% TE) are better candidates for the primary readiness signal. This is a direct, empirical caution against the common practice of headlining mRSI in athlete-facing readiness reports.

The IMTP cadence change follows the same reliability logic applied to testing frequency rather than metric choice: because IMTP's week-to-week noise (13%) is larger than its real 3–6-month change (11%), testing weekly cannot distinguish real strength change from measurement error, so a 4×/season cadence was justified and written into the time-critical `camp_2026_testing_ask.md` (camp opens within days). The classifier recalibration aligned the single-test threshold ladder with the consecutive-test ladder, moving 281 of 1,640 reds — all originating from the single-test path — into other categories; the corresponding re-run of the 10,592 already-classified production rows was deferred because it mutates production data. The session also corrected a provenance detail from the source symposium transcript: the survival-analysis content was actually Cam Josse's talk, not Patrick Ward's. The work was left as a clean, pushed, green draft PR (#1) with the merge decision deliberately deferred, and left three open questions for the user and S&C staff: (1) whether Monday IMTP is a priming stimulus rather than just measurement, (2) whether staff should stop leading with RSI-modified in favor of Peak Power/BM, and (3) the PR merge decision.

## claude.ai Firecrawl
Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts. Firecrawl provides web, developer, and research search, and executes catalogued Alexandria data providers. Use firecrawl_search to find relevant results across the web and specialized indexes; authenticated searches also return matching Alexandria providers in data.tools. firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and provider contracts; firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_scrape with a url retrieves one supplied page. For a programming question, firecrawl_developer_search searches indexed public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, READMEs, and code documentation and returns the matched passages, and skills: "only" narrows it to agent-skill files; firecrawl_search with categories: ["developer"] reaches the same index beside ordinary web results, returning the hits in the web group rather than as passages and offering no skills filter. For a biomedical, life-science, clinical, or arXiv literature question, the firecrawl_research_* tools search the paper index, while categories: ["research"] on firecrawl_search filters ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites. Use the firecrawl_research_* tools to search academic and research literature, expand from anchor papers via the citation graph, and read full-text passages from a specific paper. ## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

Route by what the user actually wants:
- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects… [truncated]

## claude.ai Supabase
Here are guidelines for using Supabase tools effectively:

- Before making schema changes, inspect the existing tables so you understand the current structure
- When debugging issues, start by reading the project's logs and its security and performance advisories before making changes
- Look up the project's API URL and its publishable API keys when helping users configure client-side integrations
- SQL runs on the project's database server. Never read server-side files or run OS commands via SQL.

If you have access to a local development environment with a filesystem and shell:
- Install the Supabase agent skill for critical development and security guidance: `npx skills add supabase/agent-skills` (https://supabase.com/docs/guides/getting-started/ai-skills.md)
- Use the Supabase CLI (`supabase`) for local development workflows such as starting a local stack, managing migrations, and running edge functions locally (https://supabase.com/docs/guides/local-development.md)
- Prefer local development and testing before applying changes to a remote project

If you are running in a web-only or remote environment without filesystem or shell access:
- Rely on the MCP tools directly for all Supabase interactions
- Apply schema migrations carefully, as changes go directly to the remote project
