# Answer-Key Audit Step in Pre-Registered Jev Tests

The answer-key audit step is a mandatory, pre-registered stage added to every Jev evaluation in `docs/JEV_CAPABILITY_MAP.md` on 2026-09-26 (commit `146fbab`, pushed to main). It requires that before the first model call, the test declare how disagreements between a confident model and the human answer key will be adjudicated — because in Eric's own history, such a disagreement has been a label error as often as a model error. The step is deliberately structured so that the audit can never rescue a failing score.

## Key Points

- **Four-part procedure, written down before the first call:** (1) pull every case where Jev is confident and disagrees with the label, at a confidence threshold fixed in advance; (2) Eric judges those cases blind and shuffled, marking each label-right / Jev-right / unclear; (3) report *both* the original-label score — which alone decides pass/fail, and whose bar never moves — and the audited score plus a label-change count; (4) cap the manual review at a random 20 cases.
- **The guardrail is the point:** a test that fails on original labels but passes after the audit is still reported **FAIL**. The audit produces grounds to re-run against fresh labels, never grounds to reclassify a result.
- **More than 20 disagreements means the labels are the finding.** Exceeding the cap escalates from "audit the test" to "the answer key warrants its own write-up," rather than expanding the review indefinitely.
- **Pre-registration is what makes it honest.** Because label errors are a known recurring phenomenon here, the audit must be declared up front; invoking it only after seeing a bad score would make it indistinguishable from motivated reinterpretation.
- **Empirical base for the step:** Jev has surfaced label errors three times in this codebase — a surgery count corrected 17→22, evidence tags where 5 of 8 disagreements sided with Jev, and role words in the spring exit notes.

## Details

A pre-registered pass bar assumes the answer key is correct, and that assumption fails in exactly the cases that matter most. When a confident model contradicts a human label, three explanations compete: the model is wrong, the label is wrong, or the case is genuinely ambiguous. A bare score collapses all three into "model error," which both understates a good model and hides a defective test set. The audit step separates them by forcing a blind, shuffled re-judgment of precisely the contested cases — blind and shuffled because the reviewer is adjudicating their own prior labels and would otherwise anchor on them.

The reporting rule is what keeps the step from becoming a loophole. Dual reporting (original-label score for the verdict, audited score plus label-change count as diagnostic) preserves the pre-registered bar's function as an immovable commitment while still surfacing what the audit learned. The explicit FAIL-stands guardrail closes the remaining gap: without it, "the labels were wrong" becomes an always-available escape hatch after any disappointing result, and the bar effectively moves every time it is missed. Instead, a post-audit pass converts into a *procedural* outcome — re-run the test against a fresh answer key — which costs the labeling work again and therefore cannot be invoked casually. The random cap of 20 serves a parallel function on the effort axis: it bounds the reviewer's workload per test and turns a high disagreement count into its own escalation signal rather than an ever-growing review queue.

A related discipline recorded the same day concerns how repeat misses are remediated: when Jev repeatedly misses the same case, the fix is **more context, not reworded prompts**. The OKRs_2026-27 tagging miss traces to that project's one-line purpose text, and permission-gate misses trace to Jev not reading script bodies — both input-completeness problems that prompt rewording would only mask.

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/pre-registered-pass-bar]] — The commitment this step extends; the audit supplies the missing treatment of a fallible answer key without letting the bar move.
- [[concepts/jev-leverage-sweep-typesafe]] — The sweep and its three admission conditions; the capability map amended here is that sweep's standing artifact.
- [[connections/cross-check-two-independent-extractions]] — The audit is this pattern applied to labels: the model's judgment and the human label are two independent derivations, and their disagreement localizes uncertainty.
- [[concepts/statistical-inference-audit-checklist]] — Shares the concern with evaluations whose design cannot license the conclusion drawn from them.
- [[connections/measured-baseline-before-model-adoption]] — Both insist the comparison object (baseline, answer key) be established fairly before the model is credited or blamed.

## Sources

- [[daily/2026-09-26.md]] — Memory-maintenance session (08:10): answer-key audit step added to `docs/JEV_CAPABILITY_MAP.md` and committed as `146fbab`; four-part procedure, fixed-in-advance confidence threshold, blind/shuffled label-right / Jev-right / unclear judgment, dual score reporting, random cap of 20, FAIL-stands guardrail, three historical label-error instances, and the "more context not reworded prompts" remediation rule.

===END ARTICLE===

# Auditing an External Claim Against One's Own Implementation

On 2026-09-26 an X post promoting a cheap Jev-based checking technique was evaluated by two separate steps: verifying the underlying source, then auditing the source's findings against the existing `TypeSafe_Sandbox` codebase. The source was legitimate — "Just Ask Jev," arXiv 2609.29429, 24 Sep 2026, code published — but the post's framing was not, and the audit showed four of the paper's five findings were already implemented. The "should we adopt this?" question was thereby converted into "we already do four of five," with the fifth ruled out on volume grounds.

## Key Points

- **Source legitimacy and framing legitimacy are independent.** The paper existed, was recent, and shipped code; the post's spin nonetheless misrepresented it on two counts — the paper tests Jev as a *checker of other models' outputs* (hallucination, jailbreak, sycophancy), and the headline "63× cheaper" is measured against LLM-as-judge on those benchmarks, not against Eric's Claude spend.
- **A mismatched baseline makes a cost claim inapplicable, not merely optimistic.** Because the comparison object was LLM-as-judge on published benchmarks, the multiple says nothing about the spend it was being invoked to reduce.
- **Provenance of the promoter is evidence.** The same account authored the post behind use case 7 (topic-routed rules), which Eric had already measured and dropped — a prior negative result about that source's recommendations.
- **Four of five findings already implemented:** source-grounded verification (`DELIVERABLE_VERIFIER.md`); threshold calibration on ~10 labeled examples (`verifier/calibrate.py`, `skill_router/calibrate.py`, t=0.15); confidence-gated action with human fallback (Fireflies tagger: 36/39 acted, 33/36 correct); and Jev surfacing label errors (observed three times).
- **The fifth was rejected on scale, not merit:** batching questions per call only pays off at volumes Eric does not reach.

## Details

The session's method is the transferable part. Rather than treating a promotional claim as either accepted or dismissed, it split the evaluation into verification of the cited artifact and an audit of that artifact's content against code already on disk. Verification alone would have produced a false positive — the paper is real, recent, and open-sourced, so a checklist stopping at "does the source exist?" would have recommended adoption. The audit is what supplied the actual answer, and it required reading the paper's findings one at a time against named files and measured numbers in the repo. The output of that audit is not a judgment of the paper but an inventory of the reader's own position relative to it.

Two failure modes were avoided. First, a headline efficiency multiple was checked for what it was measured *against*: 63× versus LLM-as-judge on hallucination/jailbreak/sycophancy benchmarks is a claim about a baseline Eric does not run, so it cannot be translated into savings on his actual spend — the same class of error as evaluating a model against a deliberately weak alternative. Second, the promoter's track record was treated as evidence: the account had previously promoted topic-routed rules, which had already been measured and dropped, meaning a prior recommendation from that source had failed an empirical test. Neither observation impugns the paper; both correctly discount the post.

The session also recorded a deferral consistent with this posture. Course-summary verification for the SCN sprint course and RTP course was logged in `docs/STATUS.md` as **open, Eric's call**, held because the 9/21 recommendation placed Jev work in maintenance mode and the three-condition admission gate requires a real downstream consumer — the test will run only if someone besides Eric (Joe, staff) actually reads those summaries. A capability being technically available is not a reason to build it.

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/jev-leverage-sweep-typesafe]] — Supplies the three admission conditions (judgment call / existing consumer / plain code measured short) and the maintenance-mode stopping point that governed the deferral here.
- [[concepts/jev-answer-key-audit-step]] — The one genuinely new practice this audit produced, added to the capability map the same session.
- [[connections/real-citations-do-not-validate-claims]] — Directly instantiated: the citation was real, and was still being used to support a claim it does not license.
- [[connections/measured-baseline-before-model-adoption]] — The "63× versus what?" question is the same demand for a fairly-specified comparison object.
- [[concepts/statistical-inference-audit-checklist]] — Catalogues the borrowed-population and incompatible-denominator errors that a cross-domain cost multiple commits.

# PP_Recruiting Workbook 012: Benchmark-Tagged Unified Grading

Workbook 012 of the PP_Recruiting project is workbook 010 plus a BENCHMARK tag and a new percentile-profile tab, completed and merged to `main` on 2026-09-26 (PR #2, merge commit `8a3de3a`). It changed no thresholds and no formulas; its purpose is to let per-position grading distributions be read off proven 2025 players. The workbook was staged for staff in `Send\`, and the session recorded three gotchas that must accompany it.

## Key Points

- **Benchmark files contained no new data.** All 710 top-2025 players were already present in the 2025 exports: 578 had zero eligibility remaining (the reason workbook 010 excluded them) and the remaining 132 were already 010 rows.
- **What 012 adds:** a BENCHMARK tag (PORTAL INPUT column BT, REVIEW BOARD column AL) and a final BENCHMARK PROFILES tab giving per-position 25th/median/75th percentiles plus share ≥75, computed live off REVIEW BOARD. Top End Speed is excluded pending mph confirmation. No thresholds or formulas were altered.
- **The data grades proven players low.** Of the 710 proven 2025 players, only 16% project AL or better, about half QS or better, and 78% still flag REVIEW — consistent with an earlier validation run. Mendoza is the exemplar: traits project FRP while a Player Impact of 98 trips REVIEW.
- **012's REVIEW count is inflated by ineligible players.** The displayed 2,352 REVIEW count drops to 010's 1,899 (1,708 with 150+ snaps) once the new Benchmark column is filtered to blank. The 011 screening-matrix numbers still refer to 010, and staff must be told this before opening 012.
- **012 is not loader-safe.** New data keeps loading onto 010, never 012 — the benchmark workbook is a read/analysis artifact, not the ingestion target.
- **Structural grading ceiling at OT/OG/C:** those positions carry only two traits each, so they can only land AA, QS, LIM, or NGE. This is a design consequence of the trait count, not a data defect.

## Details

The benchmark exercise began as an attempt to add proven-player reference data and ended by confirming that no new data existed to add — the value was entirely in tagging and summarizing rows already present. That result matters for interpretation: because the 578 zero-eligibility players were deliberately excluded from 010, tagging them back in for benchmark purposes reintroduces rows that the operational grading view intentionally omits. Hence the inflated REVIEW count and the blank-Benchmark filter that restores the operational numbers. The discipline adopted was to change nothing in the grading logic — no thresholds, no formulas — so that any difference between 010 and 012 is attributable solely to population, not to method. That is what makes the percentile profiles readable as a property of the players rather than of a revised rubric.

The substantive finding is that the grading system rates proven, productive 2025 players low: only 16% project AL or better and 78% still flag REVIEW. Mendoza makes the tension concrete — trait projections land at FRP while a Player Impact score of 98 nonetheless trips REVIEW, meaning the flag is firing on players whose production is close to the ceiling. Read together with the OT/OG/C two-trait ceiling, the pattern suggests the flagging thresholds and the trait coverage per position both need review before the REVIEW flag is treated as a screening signal. Two operational hazards were handled by file hygiene rather than documentation alone: workbook 012 was copied into `Send\` and the stale "Prototype - 003" workbook was moved to `_to_delete\`, so staff cannot open the wrong file. A STATUS correction (`a0cb038`) was pushed immediately after the merge because `main` still claimed 010 as latest, which would have hidden 010–012 from the Mac and from any fresh agent — the same cross-machine staleness problem that the machine-split closeout guards against.

Repository cleanup closed the branch: `worktree-fireflies-review-board-0915` was deleted locally and on GitHub, leaving a single-branch, clean repo. Git released the worktree cleanly, but Windows blocked deletion of the folder itself because Drive sync holds locks on `Desktop\DEV`; Eric cleared it manually, and this is expected on every worktree teardown on this laptop.

## Related Concepts

- [[concepts/playerpersonel-project-state]] — Establishes that the grading system lives in PP_Recruiting rather than PlayerPersonel; 012 is an artifact of that grading system.
- [[concepts/claude-code-worktree-gotchas]] — The Drive-sync lock blocking worktree folder deletion on `Desktop\DEV` is a new instance of this project's Windows worktree teardown friction.
- [[concepts/dev-github-drive-migration-policy]] — Explains why athlete-named recruiting artifacts are staged in local/Drive paths rather than pushed as data, and why `Desktop\DEV` is Drive-synced.
- [[concepts/machine-split-workday-closeout]] — The stale-STATUS-on-`main` problem that the `a0cb038` correction fixes is the same two-machine visibility hazard.

# Anthony Mauro Stakeholder Research Brief and the Named OKR Gate Owner

On 2026-09-26 Eric disclosed that he has been working with Anthony Mauro, Baylor football assistant general manager, and approved a professional-record research brief to prepare for that collaboration. The disclosure also resolved an ambiguity in the Applied Performance OKR set: Mauro is the "Anthony" referenced in the open gate item covering AI buy-in and data governance, which converts an unowned blocker into one with a named owner.

## Key Points

- **Scope deliberately limited to the professional record.** The brief covers background, likely evaluation habits, and what to lead with versus hold back when presenting workbook 012 — not personal information. Output goes to the repository's `docs/` directory.
- **Purpose is calibration of a deliverable, not general profiling.** "What to lead with vs. hold back in 012" makes the brief an input to how the benchmark workbook is presented, given that the grading system rates proven players low and the REVIEW count is inflated without the Benchmark-blank filter.
- **Search order is internal-then-external.** Fireflies and the SecondBrain vault are checked first — the 2026-09-15 review board meeting attributed to "a player personnel staff member" may in fact have been Mauro — before web sources (Baylor bio, LinkedIn, past bios, interviews).
- **A previously unowned OKR gate now has an owner.** The open AI buy-in / data governance item names Anthony; the pending decision is whether to fold it into the NCAA charter or park it.
- **The research was in flight, not complete,** at session end; the brief is an action item rather than a finished artifact.

## Details

The internal-before-external search order is the methodologically interesting part. Eric's own corpus already contains meetings, notes, and vault entries involving this person, but they may be filed under a generic descriptor — the 2026-09-15 review board meeting was recorded as involving "a player personnel staff member," which is exactly the kind of unattributed label that makes an internal record invisible to a name-based search. This is the retrieval failure that meeting metadata work is meant to prevent: the corpus holds the answer while the index does not expose it. Searching Fireflies and the vault first therefore serves two purposes — it surfaces first-hand observations unavailable on the public web, and it identifies which existing records need attribution corrected.

Scoping the brief to the professional record keeps a legitimate preparation exercise from drifting into surveillance of a colleague, and tying the output to a concrete question ("lead with vs. hold back in 012") supplies the stopping condition: the brief is finished when it can inform that presentation decision. The OKR consequence is the higher-leverage outcome of the disclosure. An open gate item on AI buy-in and data governance with no identified counterparty cannot be advanced — there is no one to convince and no one to negotiate governance with. Naming Mauro makes the item actionable and reduces it to a single binary decision: fold it into the NCAA charter (giving it a home and a cadence) or park it explicitly rather than leaving it to drift, which is the same forced-decision discipline the cold-project triage applies to stalled work.

# memsearch-sync ENOBUFS Hook Failure Left Unfixed by Agreement

A `memsearch-sync: index ENOBUFS` hook failure timestamped 2026-09-25 22:22 surfaced at the start of both 2026-09-26 sessions and was left unfixed in both, by explicit agreement rather than oversight. The failure was recorded as an "Open (unresolved)" item in each session's log. `ENOBUFS` is an out-of-buffer-space condition, consistent with the memsearch indexer exhausting a system resource during a sync pass.

## Key Points

- **Recurs at session start, not during work.** The failure surfaces when the hook fires at session start, meaning every new session is greeted by the same stale error until the underlying condition is cleared.
- **Deferred deliberately and recorded, not silently ignored.** Both sessions logged it as unresolved with the same timestamp, which distinguishes an accepted known defect from a lost one — the same discipline as a recorded do-not-send hold.
- **`ENOBUFS` points at resource exhaustion, not configuration.** No buffer space available is a system-resource condition, placing it alongside memsearch's history of resource-scale problems (an hours-scale first index, 81 CPU-minutes, nightly reindex relocated into the backup task) rather than alongside its PATH/timeout configuration problems.
- **Frozen timestamp implies a stale reported state.** Both occurrences cite 2026-09-25 22:22 — the error surfaced is the last recorded failure, not a fresh one per session, so its reappearance does not indicate repeated new failures.
- **A deferred hook failure has a knowledge-capture cost.** memsearch is the retrieval layer over Tier A project memory files; a broken index sync degrades cross-project recall silently while sessions proceed normally.

## Details

The operationally useful content here is the handling, not the diagnosis. Both sessions on 2026-09-26 were substantive — a capability-map amendment with a pushed commit, and a workbook merge with repo cleanup — and in both the hook error was noticed, named with its exact timestamp, and explicitly set aside. Recording a defect as open with its identifying details is what makes deferral legitimate: the next session inherits the item instead of rediscovering it, and the decision not to fix is attributable rather than accidental. This matters more for hook failures than for most errors, because hooks fail outside the conversation's work product; nothing in the session output signals that capture or indexing is degraded.

The likely cost of leaving it is a quiet retrieval gap. memsearch is what makes Tier A project memory files searchable across project contexts, which is the property that justified routing durable facts there when the global Tier B scratchpad approached its cap. If index sync is failing, newly written Tier A facts may not be retrievable even though writing them succeeded — a failure at the confirmation layer rather than the write layer, which is precisely the class of gap that requires querying the owning system rather than trusting the absence of an error. That argues for eventually verifying the index's contents directly rather than treating a clean session start as evidence the problem resolved itself. The frozen 22:22 timestamp is also a hint about the hook's reporting behavior: it appears to surface the most recent recorded failure rather than a live check, so a disappeared message would not by itself prove the indexer is healthy.

# Connection: A Verified Source Does Not License the Framing Placed On It

## The Connection

Two audits in this knowledge base reached the same structural verdict from opposite directions. On 2026-09-18, the TOS evidence brief cited real, correctly located papers and still misquoted three of them numerically, ran a Poisson cluster argument backwards, and drew causal conclusions from descriptive designs ([[concepts/tos-evidence-brief-adversarial-audit]]). On 2026-09-26, an X post cited a real, recent, code-published paper — "Just Ask Jev," arXiv 2609.29429 — and still misrepresented both its scope (a checker of *other models'* outputs) and its headline number (63× cheaper than LLM-as-judge on published benchmarks, not cheaper than the reader's own spend) ([[concepts/external-claim-audit-against-own-repo]]).

In the first case Eric was the author of the distortion; in the second he was its intended audience. The audit procedure that caught it was identical: go to the primary artifact and check what it actually measured, against what.

## Key Insight

The distortion reliably enters at the summarization boundary, and the direction of travel does not matter. A one-pager compresses a review and strips the qualifiers that constrained the claim ([[concepts/compression-amplifies-distortion]]); a promotional post compresses a paper and strips the baseline the number was measured against. Both produce an artifact that is *more quotable and less true* than its source, and in both cases the source's own legitimacy is what lends the compressed version its credibility. Checking the citation exists is therefore the cheapest and least informative verification available — it confirms the one property that was never in doubt.

The specific question that does the work is "measured against what?" A 63× cost multiple and a misquoted effect size fail the same way: the number is real somewhere, in a comparison the reader is not making. This is the cost analogue of forecast-slicing on a model's own output, where a real-looking bias is an artifact of the comparison set rather than of the thing being measured.

A practical asymmetry follows. When receiving a claim, the reader must reconstruct the source's baseline before acting — which is why the 2026-09-26 audit turned "should we adopt this?" into "we already do four of five, and the fifth doesn't apply at our volume." When *emitting* a claim, the author must propagate corrections to every derived artifact, because the compressed copies carry the distortion furthest and are the ones that get sent. One direction demands decompression; the other demands propagation.

## Evidence

- 2026-09-26 (08:10): source verified as "Just Ask Jev," arXiv 2609.29429 (24 Sep 2026), code published — "but the post's framing was hype. The paper tests Jev as a *checker of other models' outputs* … and the '63× cheaper' number is vs. LLM-as-judge on those benchmarks, not vs. Eric's Claude spend."
- 2026-09-26 (08:10): "checking the actual paper against the existing repo turned a 'should we adopt this' question into 'we already do 4 of 5'" — the audit, not the verification, produced the answer.
- 2026-09-18 (14:29): three numeric misquotes (Kamarajugadda, Ulman, scalene) and a backwards Poisson cluster argument in a brief whose citations were themselves real; the one-pagers built from it inherited the defects and were placed under the same hold.

URL mode returns markdown by default, or HTML, links, screenshots, branding data, a targeted answer, or JSON matching a supplied schema, plus page metadata. Firecrawl may serve recently indexed content; set `maxAge: 0` for a live fetch. A successful response does not by itself confirm the page is still current. Browser actions can change the live page when interactive actions are enabled, and a named browser profile can load saved session data and overwrite its stored state.

`firecrawl_search` with `sources` unset and `firecrawl_find_tools` can discover providers for the same fields across several pages; a matching Alexandria provider returns typed records in one call.

Alexandria mode: `alexandria` selects catalogued capability execution and is mutually exclusive with `url`. Alexandria execution is billed at the capability's listed price and needs a team with Alexandria enabled.

Each call may include version to pin a published workflow; omitting it uses latest. Only requestId and timeout are supported alongside alexandria. The selected contract marks required inputs and any requiresOneOf groups (at least one member per group); it may include example.request/example.response and response.key (which may differ from records). Where pagination is declared, its fields govern paging with the same filters; catalogue next is separate from provider pagination. Returns per-capability results in data.alexandria with data, records, or an error with a code; individual capabilities can fail even when the outer response succeeds. Requires an API key on a team with Alexandria enabled. Some providers require accepted terms; blocked requests return the applicable requirements.

entries.description:
Search web and specialized indexes, returning ranked results with query-relevant highlights. Each web result is a title, URL, and description. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. `includeDomains` and `excludeDomains` are mutually exclusive hostname filters; categories limit result types to `research`, `pdf`, or `developer`.

For a programming question, add `categories: ["developer"]`. It searches an index of public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation, and returns the results in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`.

Authenticated search combines web results, semantic tool summaries and domain matches. Use sources: ["alexandria"] for semantic tools only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Tool matches describe available structured-data capabilities, not executed data. toolDetail: "compact" (default) returns only provider, capability and description; "summary" adds metadata; "full" includes their input and output contracts. firecrawl_scrape with an alexandria body executes a selected capability; firecrawl_find_tools provides catalogue browsing and full contracts.

toolDetail.description: Compact by default. Compact returns only provider, capability and description; full includes contracts. Inspect selected compact tools with firecrawl_find_tools providers and capabilities.

query.description: Query for web and semantic tool discovery. Operators include quoted phrases, `-term`, `site:host`, `inurl:term`, `intitle:term`, and `related:host`; the set is non-exhaustive. Catalogue browsing is available through firecrawl_find_tools.

domainTools.description: Include domain-matched tools for result URLs. Defaults to true when Alexandria is combined with web, news or images; semantic-only search leaves domain matching off.

highlights.description: Return query-relevant page excerpts for web and news results when available (default). Highlights appear in web `description` and news `snippet`; otherwise, original snippets are returned. Set to false to keep the original search snippets.

includeDomains.description: Hostnames to restrict results to. Mutually exclusive with excludeDomains.

excludeDomains.description: Hostnames to leave out of results. Mutually exclusive with includeDomains.

sources.description: Search sources; authenticated sessions default to web + alexandria, keyless sessions to web only. A search with sources: ["web"] omits semantic provider discovery; domainTools: true can still return website-matched tools. Web-only results use domainTools: false. Use ["alexandria"] alone for provider discovery without web results.

categories.description: Limit results to specific source types. `research` restricts ordinary web results to research-affiliated websites and returns page snippets, which is separate from the `firecrawl_research_*` tools that search paper abstracts and full text across biomedical (PubMed, bioRxiv, medRxiv) and arXiv literature; `pdf` searches PDF results; `developer` searches an index built for coding agents over public repositories, GitHub issues, merged pull requests, repository READMEs, and code documentation. `developer` returns hits in `data.web` with `category: "developer"`; the other categories also filter `data.web`.
